title: What emergency response training, drills and inductions does NOPSEMA expect on offshore facilities in Australia?
description: Emergency drills, response team competence and facility induction on Australian offshore facilities under the 2024 Safety Regulations, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: Under section 2.20 of the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage (Safety) Regulations 2024, every offshore facility safety case must make adequate provision for escape and fire drills that train people to act in an emergency with adequate knowledge, preparedness and confidence. NOPSEMA's emergency planning guidance note expects a competence assurance process for emergency response roles, simulation for critical roles such as Emergency Commander, and for other workers a basic offshore safety induction, facility induction and ongoing drills.
keyTakeaways: The 2024 Safety Regulations commenced on June 12, 2025; the compilation in force as at November 2026 dates from March 31, 2026.

Section 2.20(3) to (5) requires the safety case to provide for escape drill and fire drill exercises, and the operator to ensure, as far as reasonably practicable, that they are held as the safety case says.
NOPSEMA guidance note N-04300-GN1053 (November 21, 2025) sets out three steps for emergency response competence: identification, training and assessment.
NOPSEMA says drills must consider unexpected scenarios such as blocked escape routes and failed evacuation equipment, and recommends realistic and unannounced exercises.
For workers outside the emergency response team, NOPSEMA indicates that a BOSIET course, facility induction, a facility assessment questionnaire and ongoing drills may be all that is required.
regulator: National Offshore Petroleum Safety and Environmental Management Authority (NOPSEMA)
appliesTo: Operators of offshore petroleum and greenhouse gas storage facilities in Commonwealth waters, including FPSOs, MODUs, accommodation and construction vessels
Emergency response team members, including Emergency Commander, deputy, team leaders, radio and control room operators and muster checkers
All members of the workforce and visitors present on the facility
Contractors whose personnel take part in emergency response

sections.heading: Where do offshore emergency training duties sit in Australian law?

blocks.text: They sit in Chapter 2, Subdivision C (Emergencies) of the [Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage (Safety) Regulations 2024](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2024L01588/latest/text), which describe what the facility safety case must contain about emergencies. The Regulations were registered on December 6, 2024 and commenced on June 12, 2025. The compilation current as at November 2026 shows the law as in force on March 31, 2026, after a consequential amendment.

The general workforce competence duty in section 2.9 and the command structure in section 2.8 are covered in [NOPSEMA safety case competence requirements](/regulations/nopsema-safety-case-competence-requirements). This page focuses on the emergency layer: the drill and exercise provisions in sections 2.16 to 2.20 and NOPSEMA's guidance on building emergency response competence and inductions.

Because the obligations are written as safety case content, the operator's own commitments become the inspection standard once NOPSEMA accepts the safety case. A drill schedule written into the safety case and then not followed is a compliance gap in its own right.

sections.heading: What do the emergency sections of the Safety Regulations require?

blocks.text: Five sections define the emergency arrangements that training must prepare people to use.

items: **Section 2.16, evacuation, escape and rescue analysis.** The safety case must identify the types of emergency that could arise, evaluate primary and alternative escape routes, procedures, equipment, temporary refuge amenities and life-saving equipment, including life rafts for the maximum number of persons likely to be on the facility.
**Section 2.17, fire and explosion risk analysis.** The safety case must evaluate detection, control and extinguishment measures for fires and petroleum leaks.

**Section 2.18, emergency communications.** Communications within the facility and with onshore installations, vessels, aircraft and other facilities must be adequate and protected so they work in an emergency.
**Section 2.19, control systems.** Back-up power, lighting, alarms, ballast control and emergency shutdown must be adequately provided for.

**Section 2.20, emergency preparedness.** The safety case must describe and provide for implementing an emergency response plan that specifies all reasonably practicable steps to keep people safe and the performance standards it applies.

blocks.title: The drill duty in section 2.20
blocks.text: Subsection (3): the safety case must make adequate provision for escape drill exercises and fire drill exercises by persons on the facility. Subsection (4): those exercises must ensure persons on the facility will be trained to function in an emergency with an adequate degree of knowledge, preparedness and confidence concerning the relevant emergency procedures. Subsection (5): the operator must ensure, as far as reasonably practicable, that the drills are held in accordance with the safety case.

For mobile facilities, section 2.20(6) adds systems to shut down or disconnect operations that could affect people's health or safety, with audible and visible warnings. Crews on FPSOs, MODUs and construction vessels therefore need training on disconnect alarms and procedures as well as on escape and firefighting.

sections.heading: How does NOPSEMA expect emergency response competence to be built?

blocks.text: Through a described competence assurance process. NOPSEMA's [Emergency planning guidance note, N-04300-GN1053](https://www.nopsema.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/N-04300-GN1053%20-%20Emergency%20Planning%20%28A313116%29.pdf), dated November 21, 2025, says operators must describe how competence is ensured for emergency response team members and sets out three steps:

items: **Competence identification:** what abilities and skills each individual needs, with task analysis recommended to find critical competency requirements for each role.
**Competence training:** what training develops those abilities, considering design, content and delivery methods.

**Competence assessment:** how the operator tests that training worked. NOPSEMA says "it is not sufficient to assume competency of staff after training"; assessment can include simulations, role-play, drills and exercises, or questionnaires.

blocks.text: The guidance expects operators to consider nationally and internationally recognized units of competency, noting that Offshore Petroleum Industry Training Organisation (OPITO) based standards are often used, but stresses that each facility is unique, so facility-specific training and assessment is needed on top of generic courses. The depth of training should be proportional to the criticality of the role. Simulated environment training "may be warranted" for roles such as Emergency Commander and deputy, where it can reveal stress-induced errors that other testing misses.

NOPSEMA also says the team should be trained and tested as a whole, not only as individuals, with post-exercise review and feedback, and that operators must account for skill fade because emergency skills "can easily be eroded over time if not regularly practiced". The safety case should describe refresher training and ongoing drill commitments. The [competency assessment](/glossary/competency-assessment) and [verification of competency](/guides/how-to-set-up-verification-of-competency) pages cover how to design the assessment step.

sections.heading: What induction does a worker arriving offshore need?

blocks.text: It depends on the role. For an offshore worker who is not part of the emergency team, GN1053 says completion of a basic offshore safety induction and emergency training (BOSIET) course, a facility induction, a facility assessment questionnaire and ongoing involvement in drills "may, in this case, be all that is required with respect to emergencies".

The guidance illustrates a layered induction pathway, adapted from Offshore Energies UK, that combines external and facility-specific steps. For all personnel it runs from a common induction and the employing company's induction, through a pre-flight briefing video at the heliport or facility, to a facility-specific induction and team and on-the-job induction. Personnel with emergency response duties then add onshore training programs for their specific roles and the operator's facility- and operation-specific training and assessment. Activities that would be impracticable or unsafe to practice offshore, such as helicopter underwater escape training (HUET) or firefighting, are refreshed onshore.

Designing that pathway is an induction problem as much as an emergency one; the guide on [building a safety induction](/guides/how-to-build-a-safety-induction) covers how to make each layer verifiable rather than attendance-based.

sections.heading: What makes a drill and exercise program adequate?

blocks.text: Drills should be based on the scenarios in the formal safety assessment and should demonstrate that the emergency response plan's performance standards will be met. GN1053 suggests a drill and exercise schedule with commitments for each major accident event and lists factors that determine adequacy:

items: Frequency, and coverage of all possible scenarios.
Testing of emergency communications, alarms and response equipment.
Testing of procedures, backup response measures and the decision-making framework.
Testing of individual and team performance.
Realistic and unannounced exercises at various times.
Evaluation of plan execution against the performance standards.

blocks.text: The guidance's core concepts add that emergency planning, including drills and exercises, must consider unexpected scenarios such as blocked escape routes and failure of evacuation and escape devices. It recommends a post-drill review process described in the safety case, and suggests independent observers for unbiased feedback. Drills are described as an integral part of competence assessment: they should refresh knowledge, find individual gaps and expose training system deficiencies. Operators already running [tabletop exercises](/guides/how-to-run-a-tabletop-exercise) onshore can use the same debrief structure.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links each emergency response role to the major accident events and plan procedures it supports, then to the training, drills and assessments that verify it. Drill findings feed back as gaps against named competences, which gives NOPSEMA a traceable line from section 2.20 to individual readiness. More on how this applies across the sector is on the [energy and resources](/industries/energy-resources) page.

faqs.q: How often must emergency drills be held on an Australian offshore facility?
faqs.a: The Safety Regulations do not set a fixed interval. Section 2.20 requires the safety case to make adequate provision for escape and fire drills, and the operator must ensure they are held as the safety case says. NOPSEMA's guidance treats frequency as one of the factors in judging whether the provision is adequate.

faqs.q: Is BOSIET mandatory for offshore work in Australia?
faqs.a: The Regulations do not name BOSIET. NOPSEMA's emergency planning guidance says that for workers outside the emergency response team, a BOSIET course, facility induction, facility assessment questionnaire and ongoing drills may be all that is required for emergencies. Operators commit to their own requirements in the safety case.

faqs.q: Does generic offshore emergency training satisfy NOPSEMA?
faqs.a: Not on its own. GN1053 notes that OPITO-based standards are often used, but says each facility is unique in layout, equipment, processes and procedures, so facility-specific training and assessment is needed in addition to industry-recognized generic programs.

faqs.q: Do offshore drills need to include unexpected scenarios?
faqs.a: NOPSEMA expects so. The core concepts in GN1053 say emergency planning, including drills and exercises, must consider possible unexpected scenarios such as blocked escape routes and failure of evacuation and escape devices and equipment, and the guidance lists realistic and unannounced exercises as an adequacy factor.
